candidates.caption: Chapter 1: My Husband Got His Mistress Pregnant—And Married Her Three years of trying. Three years of needles, hormones, and pain that left Vivienne Rivers hollow and aching. But finally—finally—she was pregnant. She walked into the hospital glowing, ready for her first prenatal appointment. Ready to start building the file that would track her baby's growth. The nurse at the registration desk looked up with an apologetic smile. "I'm sorry, ma'am. We can't create a file with the information you've provided." Vivienne's joy froze mid-breath. "Why not?" "Because your husband has already registered here with another woman. About two weeks ago, he came in with his wife—the woman on his marriage certificate—for her prenatal appointment and file setup. And that woman isn't you." "That's impossible." Vivienne's voice came out flat, disbelieving. "We've been married for five years. We're happy. You must have made a mistake." The nurse's expression shifted—pity, discomfort, something Vivienne couldn't name. "We don't make mistakes like that." A cold, creeping dread slithered up Vivienne's spine. The room tilted. She steadied herself against the counter, forcing her breathing to slow. It had to be a mix-up. Harrison Lancaster loved her. He wouldn't do this. Harrison had been on a business trip for two weeks. She hadn't told him about the pregnancy yet—she'd wanted it to be a surprise when he got home. This was just some clerical error. It had to be. She left the registration desk in a daze, rode the elevator down in silence. She'd go to the county clerk's office, check the marriage records herself, clear this whole thing up. The elevator doors opened. And there he was. Harrison. Walking toward her down the hospital corridor, arm wrapped around a young woman's waist. His hand rested on her stomach, fingers tracing slow, tender circles over the fabric of her dress. Vivienne ducked behind a pillar, heart hammering, and watched. The woman was Isadora Shepherd. Twenty years old. The daughter of one of Harrison's business partners. Ten years younger than Harrison. Isadora tilted her head up, fingers curling around the back of his neck, and pouted. "Honey, do you think the baby will look more like you or me?" Harrison's voice was warm, indulgent. "Like you, I hope. That way everyone will love them." They passed within feet of where Vivienne stood frozen, and neither of them noticed her. Vivienne's nails bit into her palms hard enough to draw blood, but she felt nothing. She'd never imagined Harrison could betray her. For two weeks, he'd called her every night. Told her he missed her. And the whole time, he'd been here. With her. She'd believed him. She'd let them pump her full of hormones, endured the swelling and the nausea and the endless needles, all so she could give him a child. And this was what he'd been doing. She followed them. Watched them finish the appointment, watched them leave the hospital and get into a car. She needed to know where they were going. If he had a second home with her. A second life. She hailed a cab and followed. Harrison and Isadora pulled up to an upscale club and disappeared inside, into a private room. Vivienne stood outside the door, listening. Laughter. Voices she recognized—Harrison's friends. "Dude, you two are disgusting. You can't keep your hands off each other for five minutes. You're making the rest of us jealous." "Seriously, man. You've got it made. A sweet, devoted wife at home, and a gorgeous, fun girlfriend on the side. Living the dream." Isadora's face flushed pink. She ducked her head, hiding against Harrison's chest. Harrison wrapped an arm around her, glancing up at his friends with a lazy smirk. "All right, knock it off. Izzy's shy. You're embarrassing her." A year ago, Harrison had gotten drunk at a business dinner and slept with Isadora. She'd been in love with him for three years and refused to let him go. They'd kept it going ever since. Two weeks ago, when Isadora found out she was pregnant, Harrison married her. He couldn't let his child be born out of wedlock. As for Vivienne—their marriage certificate had always been fake. Vivienne couldn't get pregnant. That's what he'd thought. She'd never pass muster with his mother or the board. She could never be Mrs. Lancaster. A man in his position needed an heir. And Vivienne was stubborn. If he hadn't dangled the promise of marriage in front of her, she never would have stayed. Luckily, she'd never questioned it. Not once in five years. Vivienne stood outside the door, her heart crushed under an invisible weight, every beat agony. Harrison's friends knew about Isadora. They called her his wife. They were comfortable with her, familiar. He'd been bringing her to events. Introducing her around. And Vivienne had never known. Inside, someone suggested a game. Isadora lost. One of Harrison's friends grinned. "All right, penalty time. You have to kiss one of the guys here. And make it good—French kiss, full commitment." Through the crack in the door, Vivienne watched Isadora glance shyly at Harrison. And then Harrison pulled her close and kissed her. Deep. Slow. Like they had all the time in the world. Vivienne felt something inside her crack open, blood pouring out into the hollow space where her heart used to be. She stood there, numb, and watched them. Harrison had told her a thousand times that he would only ever love her. That he would never touch another woman. Apparently, promises didn't mean much. She left the club like a ghost, got into another cab, and went to the county clerk's office. The clerk confirmed it. There was no marriage record. Vivienne Rivers and Harrison Lancaster had never been legally married. Before the wedding, Harrison had told her he was too busy to go to the clerk's office in person. He'd said he could have someone handle the paperwork for them. She'd trusted him. He'd had someone forge a fake certificate. Five years of marriage. All of it a lie. Every promise he'd made. Every word of love. Fake. Vivienne had graduated from college and applied for a drug development position at Lancaster Group. Harrison had seen her and fallen—or so he'd said. He'd pursued her relentlessly. She'd turned him down. She didn't believe in marriage. He wouldn't give up. He showed up everywhere. Sent her custom-designed necklaces on every holiday. Made her red-date tea by hand when she had her period. Changed all his social media handles to her initials. His intensity, his tenderness—it wore her down. But she still wouldn't admit she loved him. Then they went skiing in Greymont. There was an avalanche. Harrison threw himself over her, shielding her with his body. She walked away without a scratch. He spent a month in the ICU. After that, she couldn't deny it anymore. She loved him. She wanted to love him the way he loved her. When she couldn't get pregnant, his mother turned cold. Vivienne didn't want Harrison caught in the middle, so she quit her job and focused on fertility treatments. She took the pills, endured the injections, even when the injection sites swelled and hardened, even when the hormones wrecked her body. She never gave up. And when she finally got pregnant, when she was ready to share the news— He gave her this. She went back to the hospital. Got a new appointment number. The doctor looked at her chart, then up at her face. "Are you sure you want to terminate?" Vivienne's hand drifted to her stomach. Her eyes were empty. She nodded. If Harrison had cheated, she was done. She wouldn't keep him. And she wouldn't keep his child. The doctor nodded. "All right. We'll need to run some tests first. Once we have the results, we'll schedule the procedure." Vivienne took the paperwork, paid the fee, went through the tests. While she waited for the results, her phone buzzed. A video call. Harrison. She almost declined. Then her thumb slipped. The call connected. Harrison's face filled the screen, handsome and warm, his eyes full of the same affection they'd always held. "Vivi, why are you at the hospital? Are you feeling okay?" Chapter 2: Why the Sudden Job? Seeing the hospital in the background, Harrison's voice filled with concern. Vivienne caught the worry in his tone and felt a flicker of confusion. She couldn't tell anymore whether he was sincere or just that good at pretending. When she didn't answer, he assumed she was too sick to speak, and his anxiety spiked. "Vivi, I'm coming right now. Wait for me." Thinking back to what he'd said in that private room, Vivienne wanted nothing more than to reach through the screen and slap him. But she was also afraid that if he came now and found out she was pregnant, he'd stop her from going through with the procedure. So she forced herself to act like nothing was wrong. "You don't need to come. I'm fine. I'm just here with Juliette—she's getting her stomach checked. Focus on work. Don't worry about me." Juliette Sinclair was Vivienne's best friend. The two of them went out for meals and coffee all the time, and Harrison had met her before. Hearing it was Juliette who was sick, Harrison relaxed. His voice softened. "All right. But don't wear yourself out. I'd hate that. Tell you what—I'll wrap things up early and come home this weekend. Wait for me." Vivienne laughed bitterly to herself. She didn't believe a word of it, but her expression stayed the same as always. "Okay. I'll wait for you." "I love you, Vivi." After hanging up, Vivienne went to pick up her test results, then headed to the consultation room. The doctor reviewed the results and frowned. "Your uterine lining is thin. You already have difficulty conceiving. If you go through with the procedure, it could cause permanent damage to your endometrium. You might never be able to have children." Vivienne's heart clenched. Her hand moved to her stomach. If she didn't keep this baby, would she never get to be a mother? The doctor looked at her. "Why don't you think it over? This is a big decision. You should talk to your family." Vivienne didn't know if she'd regret this later. She could live without Harrison. But she didn't want to lose the chance to be a mother. Walking out of the hospital, she stared up at the overcast sky and let out a bitter smile. Just then, a car sped past, nearly clipping her. She stumbled, about to fall, when a strong hand caught her waist and steadied her. She looked up and met a pair of deep, dark eyes. The roar of an engine filled her ears. Vivienne snapped back to herself and quickly pulled away from the man's arms, her voice a little flustered. "Thank you." The man had sharp features, a tall frame, and wore a tailored suit. His presence was commanding, the kind that came from years at the top. One look at him and you knew he was someone important. Vivienne glanced at him once and immediately felt out of her depth. Declan Palmer saw that she was steady on her feet. His voice was calm and measured. "No need to thank me." His tone was low and slightly accented, but pleasant to the ear. A respectful voice came from behind him. "Mr. Palmer, the car's here. We need to leave now if we're going to make the flight." Declan gave Vivienne a polite nod and walked toward a stretch Rolls-Royce. His assistant opened the door, and he climbed inside with long strides. After the car had been driving for a while, the assistant spoke. "Mr. Palmer, we still haven't found that woman here in Riverbend. Should we keep looking?" Declan rubbed his temples, exhausted. "Keep looking. My grandmother's condition—only she can treat it." "Understood." When Vivienne got home, the housekeeper, Aunt Chapman, came forward to take her bag and asked with concern, "Ma'am, where were you today? Mr. Lancaster called earlier asking if you were back yet." Vivienne's tone was flat. "I'm fine. I just went out with a friend. By the way, Aunt Chapman, I'm planning to take a trip for a few days. You can take some time off too." Aunt Chapman looked surprised. "But Mr. Lancaster is coming home this weekend. Why don't you wait until he's back, then go?" Usually, ma'am hardly ever went out. She'd stay in the study reading or researching herbal remedies to help with conception. Why was she acting so strange today? Something felt off. Aunt Chapman decided she'd call Mr. Lancaster later to let him know. After all, before he left on his trip, he'd told her over and over to take good care of his wife. Vivienne's expression grew colder at her words. Aunt Chapman was the eighth housekeeper they'd hired. She was better than the others in that she didn't take advantage of Vivienne's youth to slack off or cut corners behind her back. But like all the rest, she listened to Harrison more than she listened to Vivienne. Vivienne's tone sharpened. "I said I'm going on a trip for a few days and you're taking time off. Do I need your permission to make my own decisions? Pack your things and go home. You don't need to make dinner." Aunt Chapman rarely saw her speak so harshly. She was annoyed, but she nodded reluctantly. "Yes, ma'am." Inside, she couldn't help but grumble. A woman from nothing, no job, who married up and can't even have a baby—who knows if she'll get kicked out one day. What's she acting so high and mighty for? Back in the bedroom, Vivienne started packing. They'd been together for five years. Every corner of the room held memories of their life together. Thick photo albums, souvenirs from trips, ceramic pieces they'd made together—she threw it all away. The designer jewelry, clothes, and accessories he'd given her—she wouldn't take them, but she wasn't going to let Isadora have them either. She took photos of everything and listed them for sale on a resale platform. Then she packed up the things she'd brought into the marriage and put them in her suitcase. She also sealed up the precious medical texts her grandfather had left her and packed them into boxes. Before the wedding, she'd used the savings her grandfather left her to buy a small apartment in Riverbend. She called a moving company to take everything there. Only after it was all gone did she check her phone and see that Harrison had called eighteen times and sent her messages. In his texts, he asked, "Aunt Chapman said you're going on a trip. What's going on? You don't like going out. No, I don't feel good about this. Wait until I get back and I'll go with you." Vivienne stared at the message, her eyes full of scorn. He really was a master of time management—taking care of his pregnant mistress while still finding time to check in on her. She was afraid Harrison would come back suddenly and ruin her plans, so she swallowed her anger and replied, "Juliette's boyfriend cheated on her. She's a mess. She drank so much she ended up in the hospital. I want to take her to a nearby city to clear her head." Harrison replied quickly. "Got it. My wife's so loyal. Take good care of her. If you need money, spend whatever you want. Don't try to save for me. I work so I can spoil you." Right after she read the message, her phone buzzed with a transfer notification. Two hundred thousand dollars. Vivienne thought back over the past three years. Every time he was away for more than three days, he'd find some excuse to send her money—large amounts, too. Never less than a hundred thousand. Now she understood. It was guilt money. He was trying to buy her off. Suddenly, she couldn't help but ask him, "Do you think all men get bored eventually? Harrison, if you ever got tired of me, would you cheat on me too?" She waited three minutes before he replied. "Vivi, I'm not like other men. I would never betray you. I, Harrison, only love Vivienne. No one else." Vivienne stared at the message. Her hand trembled around the phone. If she hadn't gone to the hospital for that checkup and learned the truth, she never would have known that the man she slept beside every night was such a liar. Were all men like this? One thing to your face, another behind your back? But she wasn't going to let him off easy. Even without a marriage certificate, she was going to take half of everything he had. All the pain she'd felt in this relationship—she'd make him and Isadora pay it back double. After uploading photos of all the bags, clothes, and jewelry she planned to sell, she felt completely drained. Pregnancy made her tired so easily. Between packing, running around, and the emotional roller coaster, she was wiped out. She lay down on the bed and fell into a deep sleep. The next morning, she woke up to more than a dozen messages from Harrison. She ignored them. But when she saw that Vice President Quincy from Lancaster Group's R&D department had also called her twice, she answered. Vice President Quincy's tone was very polite. "Ma'am, we've run into an issue with one of the formulas we're developing. We were hoping you could take a look." Vivienne's grandfather had been a legend in traditional medicine. Even in semi-retirement, patients in high places and renowned figures in the field still sought him out. In traditional medicine families, knowledge was usually passed down to children and disciples. Vivienne had studied under her grandfather since childhood, and her talent surpassed even her father's and aunt's. In college, Vivienne majored in pharmacology. After graduation, she applied to Lancaster Group. Vice President Quincy had visited her grandfather years ago and recognized her immediately as the little girl who used to follow Old Master Rivers around. He hired her on the spot. In R&D, she'd always been valued, but aside from Vice President Quincy, everyone else ostracized her. Behind her back, they said she only got ahead because of connections. After she got together with Harrison, the rumors got even worse. One time, Harrison overheard someone talking about her in the break room. He fired the employee on the spot and gave Vivienne the title of R&D Director. Harrison figured that even if she couldn't handle the role, as long as it made her happy, what was the harm in letting her play director? But he didn't know that several of the company's flagship traditional medicine products for chronic conditions had been developed under her leadership. Even after she left the company, she'd quietly kept up with R&D's work, often guiding Vice President Quincy on adjustments to development plans. She didn't care about recognition or profit. She just wanted to help patients and give them their health back. Vivienne fought through her morning sickness, opened her laptop, and reviewed the formula Vice President Quincy had sent. She found the problem. Two hours later, she'd identified the issue. Vice President Quincy was thrilled. "Thank you so much, ma'am. R&D is truly at a loss without you!" Sometimes he wished Vivienne had been born a boy. Then she could have stayed in R&D. What a shame. She was a woman, so all she could do was stay home and focus on family and children. Vivienne opened her thermos, took a sip of water to settle her stomach, then said to Vice President Quincy, "Vice President Quincy, I'm planning to come back to work at the company." She didn't want to be kept at home by Harrison anymore, clueless about what was happening at the company. She needed to understand the company's situation if she was going to take what was hers from Harrison's assets. Vice President Quincy was delighted to hear it, but at the same time, he felt uneasy. Harrison had been openly parading around the office with that Ms. Shepherd. If Vivienne came in and saw them, wouldn't she be upset? But Harrison was his boss. He couldn't exactly expose him. All he could do was hint gently. "Ma'am, maybe you should discuss it with Mr. Lancaster first?" Vivienne knew that everyone saw her as a trophy wife. They thought she couldn't do anything without Harrison's permission. This time, she was going to prove to everyone that she, Vivienne, was not some pampered, useless rose. "No need. I can take responsibility for my own decisions. Harrison told me before that even if I left to focus on family, he'd always keep the R&D Director position open for me. So I'm not applying for a job—I'm just going back to work." ****** That evening, Vivienne started preparing her work materials. She hadn't worked in three years, but she'd never stopped learning. Her skills were as sharp as ever. Then Harrison called. She felt a wave of disgust but answered as if nothing was wrong. Harrison's voice was warm. "Baby, have you been eating properly while you've been out with your friend?" Vivienne gave a noncommittal hum. Harrison continued, "I heard from Vice President Quincy that you're planning to come into the office next week. Why the sudden interest in going back to work?" Vivienne had an excuse ready. "I've been trying to get pregnant at home with no luck. The doctor suggested I change my environment and my mindset, stop being so anxious. Maybe then I'll conceive." Harrison laughed. "Baby, even if we never have kids, I'll still love you just the same. If you want a change of pace, going to work is fine. I'll tell the R&D team to take good care of you and not bother you too much. You can treat it like you're just there to have fun." Vivienne knew he'd never believed in her professional abilities. He didn't think she could contribute anything to the company. To him, she was just a canary in a cage—something pretty to look at and play with when he was bored. She let out a cold laugh. "Fine. As long as you don't mind me going to work." Then Isadora's voice came through the line. "Harry, can you blow-dry my hair?" The call cut off abruptly. Vivienne stared at her phone, her eyes full of mockery. They really were inseparable, weren't they? A moment later, Harrison called back, his voice no longer calm. "Vivi, Isadora's dad brought her along on this trip. I was just in his hotel room talking business, and she came in to mess around. You know how young girls are—always trying to get attention. Don't misunderstand." Vivienne dug her nails into her palm and forced herself to sound unbothered. "Why would I misunderstand? Isadora's just a kid. Even if you were going to cheat, you wouldn't pick someone that young, right?" Harrison couldn't help but laugh nervously. "What are you even talking about? How could I ever cheat?" He coughed. "I've been so busy with work these past few days, I haven't had time for you. Tell you what—I'll have my assistant buy you a piece of jewelry. Consider it my way of making it up to you." Vivienne hummed in acknowledgment. After hanging up, Harrison glanced at Isadora, who stood beside him in a slip nightgown, and raised an eyebrow. He and Vivienne had been together for five years. Vivienne had always been reserved in bed, and though he respected that, it left him unsatisfied. But Isadora was different. She was young, passionate, and a much better match for him in that way. Still, Vivienne was the first woman he'd ever truly liked, the first he'd seriously pursued. They had beautiful memories together. Even now that he had Isadora, he wasn't going to let Vivienne go. Isadora saw him spacing out and walked over, annoyed, wrapping her arms around his neck. "Harry..." His phone rang. Harrison dodged her kiss and answered his assistant's call. "Mr. Lancaster, we've confirmed it. Your wife wasn't at the hospital with a friend yesterday. She went alone. She had an appointment in obstetrics..." Harrison frowned. Could Vivienne be pregnant? Chapter 3: Let Her Help Discipline the Kid Later But almost immediately, he dismissed the thought. They'd done premarital health screenings back then. Vivienne's chances of getting pregnant were less than one percent. That was the whole reason he'd agreed to the fake marriage certificate in the first place. Still, thinking about how she'd gone to the hospital alone for tests and kept it from him—she must not have wanted him to worry—and here he was, keeping Isadora company instead. A pang of guilt for Vivienne stirred in Harrison's chest. He turned to Isadora. "I'm going home Saturday to be with Vivi. If you're not comfortable staying alone, you can go back to the Old Estate. My mom would be happy to look after you." Ever since learning Isadora was pregnant, his mother Rosalind Wallace had been thrilled. She used to nag him constantly about finding a woman to give her grandchildren. At least now she'd finally stopped. Isadora wasn't pleased, but she knew better than to show it. Harrison might be doting on her now, but Vivienne still had a place in his heart. If she came across as too hostile toward Vivienne, it would only backfire. She pouted playfully. "I'll do whatever you say. But I'm really going to miss you. Can I come home with you?" Harrison frowned. Before, when he and Isadora were just fooling around, bringing her back occasionally hadn't been a problem. Isadora knew to keep her mouth shut. But things were different now. Since they'd gotten their certificate, Isadora had grown bolder, clingier. He was worried her behavior might make Vivienne suspicious. Isadora could read his hesitation. She rushed to reassure him. "I promise I won't let Vivienne find out about us. I've been back before and she never noticed, right?" Worn down by her pleading, Harrison finally agreed. ****** Saturday afternoon, Vivienne had just shipped out two designer bags she'd sold when Harrison and Isadora walked in together, rolling their suitcases behind them. Isadora's tone was sweet and obedient when she saw Vivienne. "Vivienne, sorry to impose again. My parents are traveling and I don't want to be home alone. Would it be okay if I stayed here for a while?" It was the same excuse Isadora had used countless times before. In the past, Vivienne had never suspected anything between her and Harrison. She'd always been kind to Isadora. But this time, Vivienne just looked at her coolly and said nothing. Isadora couldn't read her mood. She tugged discreetly at Harrison's sleeve, hoping he'd speak up for her. Afraid Vivienne would catch on, Harrison pulled away and stepped forward to check on Vivienne instead. "Baby, I'm home. Are you sure you're feeling okay? My assistant told me everything. You didn't go to the hospital with Juliette for her checkup—you went for yourself. And you haven't been traveling these past few days, you've been home. If something's wrong, don't hide it from me. We'll deal with it together." Vivienne hadn't expected that even with Aunt Chapman gone, Harrison would have his assistant spying on her. Good thing she'd deleted all her prenatal records ahead of time. There was no way Harrison could find out. She dug her nails into her palm, keeping her expression calm. "I'm fine. Just a little cold. I went to the hospital for some medicine and came right back. I didn't tell you because I didn't want you to worry." Harrison started to press further, but Vivienne changed the subject. "Enough. Stop fussing over me. Give me your coat, I'll hang it up for you." Harrison shrugged off his coat and handed it to her. Vivienne took it and went to hang it up. Then she caught it—Isadora's perfume, clinging to the fabric. A sharp, needling pain pierced her chest. Watching Vivienne play the dutiful wife, hanging up Harrison's coat, Isadora felt a twist of irritation. She couldn't help asking, "Where's Aunt Chapman? Is she on vacation? What are we going to do about dinner?" Harrison chimed in. "You've been home all these days without anyone cooking. You probably haven't been eating properly, have you?" Vivienne's tone was flat. "I'm not that delicate. I can make simple meals myself." Isadora's eyes widened with exaggerated curiosity. "Wow, Vivienne, you can cook? I wonder if I'll be lucky enough to try your food while I'm staying here." Harrison's priorities had already shifted toward the child in Isadora's belly. He nodded in agreement. "Yeah, Vivi. Isadora's never cooked a day in her life. If you have time, you can make something for her too." Vivienne's expression went cold. This was the man she'd loved for five years. He'd given her a sham marriage. And now he was bringing his pregnant mistress home and expecting her to cook for her. What did he think she was? She'd been on the fence about going after her share of the marital assets. Not anymore. She was going to take every cent she was owed. "Sure. Give me a few minutes. I'll get started." While Vivienne cooked, Harrison and Isadora sat in the living room watching TV. Harrison didn't offer to help. In his mind, cooking wasn't that hard. Making money was way more exhausting. Vivienne lived comfortably at home with nothing to do. Making a meal now and then was no big deal. When Vivienne came out after finishing, she found the coffee table trashed—chips and crackers scattered everywhere. Neither of them had bothered to clean up. Her carefully chosen cream-colored tablecloth was stained with drink spills. Isadora set down her snack and smiled at Vivienne. "Vivienne, you're done! Let me help you set the table." She stood up and nearly stumbled. Harrison caught her quickly, his eyes dropping to her belly, his tone sharp. "Don't make trouble. Just sit and wait for dinner. You think we need you doing chores?" Isadora stuck her tongue out. "Okay, okay." Vivienne watched the two of them, nausea rising in her throat. At dinner, Isadora tried the ribs and the fish. Both were way too salty. She couldn't eat it. "Vivienne, why is everything so salty?" Vivienne ate the one dish that wasn't oversalted—the greens—her tone indifferent. "Is it? I must've added too much salt by accident." Harrison, however, said, "I think Vivi did a great job. She'll get better with practice." All Vivienne needed was encouragement. Her cooking would improve over time. He wanted her to focus on the home, not on work. Besides, Isadora was spoiled. Even after the baby was born, she probably wouldn't be able to raise it properly. Vivienne was sensible. If they gave her the child to care for and educate, it would be good for the kid. She couldn't have children of her own anyway. She'd probably be desperate for a child to keep her company. When the time came, they'd just have Isadora's baby call Vivienne godmother and let the kid live here naturally. Vivienne couldn't stomach another bite. She excused herself and went back to the bedroom. Once Vivienne was gone, Isadora whined to Harrison. "Harry, I really can't eat this." Harrison set down his chopsticks and coaxed her. "I'll have my assistant bring food over. Wait here. I need to talk to Vivi about something." Isadora was annoyed, but she knew better than to push it. If she went too far, Harrison might actually get angry. So she nodded obediently and didn't make a fuss. Harrison went into the master bedroom. Seeing the bathroom door closed, he stepped into the walk-in closet to change. Inside, he noticed that a lot of Vivienne's clothes and bags were missing. An uneasy feeling crept over him. When Vivienne came out, he asked quickly, "Vivi, where are your clothes and bags?" Chapter 4: He'd Been Drugging Her Vivienne had her excuse ready. Her voice was flat, unbothered. "I'm planning to go back to work. My old clothes weren't professional enough, so I cleared them out. I'm starting fresh. You're not going to lecture me about wasting money, are you?" Something in Harrison's expression eased. "Of course not. Buy whatever you want. If you don't like something, get rid of it." He knew Vivienne had always been careful with money. The allowance he gave her — she barely touched most of it. This was the first time she'd ever done something like this, thrown out so much at once. But those clothes and bags were years old. If she wanted them gone, fine. If anything, she'd probably regret it herself eventually, and that would be the end of her splurging. Vivienne had no interest in continuing the conversation. She walked back to the desk and pulled up the product files Vice President Quincy had sent over. Every other time Harrison came home from a business trip, she'd been all over him — clinging, talking his ear off, just happy he was back. Not tonight. Tonight she was distant, like his return meant nothing to her. And somehow, that got under his skin. Seing her like this took him back. Back to the beginning, when he'd first started pursuing her. She'd been exactly this cold then. Young, but with a stubbornness and reserve he hadn't seen in any of the other well-bred women he'd known. It had hoked him immediately. He'd chased her. She'd avoided him. And the more she pulled away, the more he wanted her. He'd finally caught her, and for a while, things had been good between them — genuinely sweet. But somewhere along the way, something had gone flat. He couldn't name when it happened. Then Isadora came along, and he understood: what he had with Vivienne was too settled, too safe. It lacked spark. Now, watching Vivienne slip back into that cool, untouchable version of herself, he felt the old pull return. He wanted to get a reaction out of her. Maybe that was just how men were wired. The colder you ran, the more interesting you became. He stepped toward her, reaching to pull her close. Vivienne felt him coming and went rigid. When she'd loved him, she'd wanted to be near him every second. But the moment she found out about his betrayal, that love had simply stopped. Like a light switching off. Now his presence, the smell of him — it turned her stomach. She stepped aside and redirected. "Harrison, I want to buy a car. Something practical for commuting." "Sure," he said without hesitating. "Pick what you want. I'll cover it." He leaned in to kiss her. She put her hand over his mouth. She watched suspicion begin to surface in his eyes and forced herself to play it soft, tilting her head with a practiced pout. "Harrison, I still have that cold, remember? You just got back — you've got to have a mountain of things to deal with at the office. I can't get you sick. And the cold medicine is already hitting me. I'm exhausted. I need to sleep." Harison considered it. If he caught her cold and passed it to Isadora, that was a risk to the baby. He let the idea go and reached over to brush his hand through Vivienne's hair, his voice still gentle. "Alright. Get some rest. I'll step out and return a few calls." She watched him leave the bedroom. Then, quietly, she followed. Harrison went into Isadora's room. The door didn't latch all the way behind him. Vivienne stood just outside and listened. "Harry — did you give Vivienne the sleeping pills? If she's not out, we need to be careful. We can't afford to get caught." "She took cold medicine. She's probably already asleep. We don't need the pills tonight. Chapter 5: Why Don't I Just Give You to Her Too? The rustle of clothing drifted through the bedroom wall. Vivienne stood in the hallway, phone in hand, recording the two of them kissing. Her palm was ice cold. She hadn't seen this coming. After Harrison brought Isadora home, he'd actually drugged her — his own wife — with sleeping pills just so he could sneak around with her. When she had enough footage, she slipped back into the bedroom without a sound. She pulled the vitamin C bottle from the cabinet, popped the cap, and shook one tablet into a glass of warm water. Then she reached for the iodine and added a few drops. She had a pharmacy degree. She knew exactly how to tell the difference. Vitamin C would decolorize iodine almost instantly — the brown would vanish right before your eyes. The water didn't react at all. So these were never vitamin C tablets. The headaches. The drowsiness. The low moods that had been dragging her down for months — she'd blamed it on anxiety, on the stress of not being able to get pregnant. Now she knew. Those were side effects of long-term sedative use. And Harrison had done this to her. A cold wave of fear moved through her. For the past two weeks, while he was supposedly away on business, she hadn't taken the pills — no one had been there to remind her. If he'd been home, she would have kept taking them. And the damage to the baby she was now carrying would have been severe. The thought made her hatred for him sharpen into something almost unbearable. He hadn't just betrayed their marriage. He'd been poisoning her body without a second thought. She pressed a hand to her stomach, and a hollow sadness settled over her. If her child ever grew up and learned what kind of man his father was, she'd rather he had never been born at all. She unlocked her phone and pulled up the clinic's booking page, ready to schedule a termination — and then it rang. Grandma. After her father died, her mother had remarried and walked away. It was her grandparents who raised her, and she'd been close to them her whole life. When her grandfather passed during her college years, her aunt had brought Grandma to Riverbend to live with the family. Vivienne had stayed in Riverbend after graduation partly for that reason — to be nearby, to take care of her. But after marrying Harrison, she'd been consumed by fertility treatments, always exhausted, always pale. She hadn't wanted to worry the old woman. Her visits had grown fewer and fewer. The guilt of that sat heavy in her chest. "Vivi, tomorrow's your aunt's birthday. Come over if you and Harrison are free." The last thing she wanted was to spend another minute pretending alongside Harrison. But for Grandma's sake, she said yes. The next morning, she came downstairs to find Harrison and Isadora already dressed and seated at the dining table, waiting. Harrison looked up with a smile. "Morning. We've been waiting on you. Feeling better? How's that cold?" Vivienne said nothing, just made a flat sound of acknowledgment and sat down across from him. The table was full of food. Isadora seized the moment. "Harry made all of this — he was up early cooking. Vivienne, I'm so jealous. You really found yourself a good husband." Vivienne looked over the spread. Tamagoyaki. Rice balls wrapped in seaweed. Miso soup. Grilled fish. None of it was anything they ever ate at home. So it was obvious who he'd made it for. "I thought you only knew how to make pasta," she said, looking at Harrison. "When did you learn all this?" He cleared his throat. "It's mostly pre-made stuff. Didn't take much. Just eat before it gets cold." She had no appetite. She took a sip of the miso soup, set down the spoon, and mentioned her grandmother's invitation. Harrison nodded. "I haven't been to see your grandma and aunt in a while. I'm free today — let's go together." After breakfast, Vivienne went upstairs to change. When she came back down, Isadora was beaming at the door. "I'll hold down the fort while you're out. Maybe tidy up a little." "Don't bother," Harrison said. "Watch TV, find something to snack on. If you get hungry for lunch, I'll have my assistant bring something over." Isadora nodded, all wide eyes and sweetness. "I'll be fine, Harry. Stop worrying about me. Go — Vivienne's waiting." He still lingered, reminding her of a few more things before finally heading out. Vivienne didn't wait for him. She got in the car and settled into the passenger seat — and noticed a notebook on the console. She picked it up and flipped it open. Isadora's handwriting. One Hundred Wishes for Me and Harry — March 2nd, my birthday. I want to see the northern lights in the Arctic with Harry and kiss him for ten minutes straight. May 20th. I want Harry to fill Victoria Harbour with fireworks for me and get down on one knee. July 14th. I want to go skydiving in Ashford Isles with Harry. I'll wear a wedding dress and we'll jump together from fifteen thousand feet. He'll never forget that day for the rest of his life. Page after page. A hundred of them. The tears came before she could stop them. All those trips he'd taken for "work." He'd been doing this — building a whole other life with her, checking off wishes one by one. After their wedding, the romance had just... stopped. No more surprises. He barely even brought her flowers anymore. Whenever she saw couples going viral online for some grand gesture, Harrison would furrow his brow and say, "Vivi, we're not like them. We don't need all that to prove what we have. Quiet and steady — that's us." He hadn't lost his sense of romance. He'd just been saving it for someone else. She shoved the notebook back into the compartment and pressed a tissue to her eyes. Harrison got in a moment later. He took one look at her red-rimmed eyes. "Vivi — have you been crying?" She forced a small smile and swallowed everything down. "No. Something flew into my eye." He nodded and started the car. They were two intersections away from her aunt's neighborhood when his phone rang. He answered. The voice on the other end was from building management. "Mr. Lancaster, the smoke alarm at your property has been triggered. We went over to check, but no one answered the door. We wanted to confirm — are you and your family out of the house?" Harrison's expression shifted. Isadora was still home. He pulled over immediately and turned to Vivienne. "I'm sorry, Vivi. The alarm went off and Isadora's still inside — I have to go back. Head to your aunt's without me. I'll come find you once I know everything's okay." Before she could get a word out, he'd already unclipped her seatbelt and was pushing her out of the car. The door shut. The car pulled away. Vivienne stood alone on the empty road and watched it go. A short, bitter laugh escaped her. The house ran on gas, and every appliance in it was top of the line — nothing had ever malfunctioned, not once. And somehow Isadora had managed to set off the smoke alarm? Of course she had. Because that was the point. He had never once left her stranded on the side of the road for any emergency before. Not once. But for Isadora, he'd made an exception. Standing there, she finally understood — clearly, completely — just how little she meant to him now that someone else had taken her place. She looked around. Waited ten minutes. Not a single cab passed. Her aunt and uncle lived in a cheaper part of town, the kind of neighborhood where you couldn't count on finding a ride. She had no choice. She walked. Forty minutes later, she arrived at the complex, wiped the sweat from her forehead, and rang the bell. From inside came the sound of a man shouting, and a woman crying — sharp, ragged sobs. Vivienne's chest tightened. She was about to knock when the door swung open. Her uncle stormed out, didn't even glance at her, and walked away fast. She stepped inside. Her aunt was on the couch, crying. Her grandmother stood to the side with her arm around Vivienne's younger cousin, eyes red. The room was a mess. Vivienne cleared the floor first — she didn't want anyone stepping on something and getting hurt — then went to the kitchen and made lunch for everyone. Afterward, her cousin took her aunt to lie down. Vivienne sat with her grandmother. Grandma took her hand and spoke in a low, worn-out voice. "Your aunt's always been too proud. Always at the hospital, never home. Can't blame your uncle for straying. Now she's talking divorce, wants him out with nothing. He won't agree, so she made a scene. What's the point of all that? If he's willing to come back, just make it work. Your aunt doesn't know what's good for her. A woman raising a child alone — who's going to want her after this?" Vivienne didn't agree with a word of it. "Grandma, Uncle did something wrong. Aunt wants a divorce. Why are you taking his side?" Grandma clicked her tongue. "You think divorce is that simple? Your cousin's still in school — tuition is twenty to thirty thousand a semester. Can your aunt cover that alone? The mortgage isn't paid off. They need two incomes for that." "Even so, he's the one who cheated. If Aunt stays with him after this, how is she supposed to live with that?" "Men are like that." Grandma waved a hand. "Your aunt only had one child and refused to have more. No son in the house — how do you expect things to go? And she brought me here to live with her instead of taking care of his mother. His mother's still back in the countryside. Of course he's unhappy. Really, it's my fault too. I should go back to the village..." She trailed off, eyes going red again, thinking of her son — Vivienne's father — gone too soon. Living in her daughter's house, she'd always felt like a guest who'd overstayed. Vivienne knew her grandmother's thinking was shaped by a different era. She'd had this argument before and never won it. But she tried anyway. "Grandma, sons and daughters are the same. Either one can take care of their parents. And his mother didn't want to come here — that's why you came to help with my cousin. You've been doing the housework, the school pickups, everything. You've given so much to this family. Aunt and Uncle should be grateful to you. If his mother had done half of what you do, Aunt wouldn't be distant with her." "Listen to you, talking nonsense." Grandma squeezed her hand, voice softening into something urgent. "Vivi, don't pick up your aunt's stubbornness. A married woman needs to be gentle, needs to keep the home together. Let this be a lesson to you. Take care of Harrison. Give him a son — soon. Don't be one of those foolish girls who decides not to have children. A son is what holds a family together. It's what keeps a man's heart at home, with you and the baby..." Something pressed down hard on Vivienne's chest. She'd been about to tell Grandma everything — about Harrison, about what she'd found. But watching her grandmother defend her uncle without hesitation, she didn't know where to begin. She said nothing. That evening, she came home to find Harrison and Isadora on the couch together, laughing, eating instant noodles. Harrison used to refuse instant noodles. Called them junk food, not worth eating. Apparently that had changed too. When he saw Vivienne walk in, he seemed to remember. He stood up quickly. "Sorry, Vivi. Isadora twisted her ankle, and I stayed to look after her. I forgot about your aunt's." Vivienne was tired. She didn't have the energy to watch them perform. She turned toward the master bedroom. Harrison caught her sleeve. "Isadora was burning some old photos this afternoon and the curtains in the guest room caught fire. I got back just in time — nothing serious. But the guest room's not usable now, and with her ankle the way it is..." He paused. "The only room left on this floor is the master. What if we move upstairs and let her have it?" When he'd come home and found Isadora alone in the room, burning photographs of the two of them, tears running down her face, something in him had cracked open. She was pregnant — her emotions were fragile. He'd felt guilty, and so he'd stayed. He'd forgotten Vivienne entirely. Vivienne looked back at Isadora. The nerve of her. Walking into their home was one thing. Now she wanted the master bedroom too. She turned back to Harrison, her voice perfectly calm. "If I'm already giving up the bedroom," she said, "why don't I just give you to her too? Chapter 6: Saving Old Madam Palmer Harrison's expression darkened. "Vivi, why do you have to be so sharp about everything? Isadora is someone we've watched grow up." Isadora pushed herself up from the couch, eyes red. "It's fine. Maybe I should just move out." Harrison stepped forward and caught her arm before she could go anywhere. "It's late. You're alone, and you twisted your ankle. Where would you even go?" Isadora dropped her gaze and said nothing. Harrison turned back to Vivienne, his voice edged with irritation. "This villa was bought with my money. I think that gives me the right to decide who sleeps in the master bedroom. You don't get a say in that." Vivienne almost laughed. When they'd first gotten married, he'd promised her that everything in his name was hers to share — that she could do whatever she wanted with it. Now he was standing here telling her she had no say over a single bedroom. She was done. She turned and walked to the entryway, crouching down to change her shoes. Harrison watched her, his irritation sharpening. "What are you doing?" Her face was blank, like she was looking at a stranger. "If this villa is yours and I have no say in it, then I'll go find somewhere I do." It had been so long since she'd pushed back on anything that he didn't quite know what to do with it. After they married, she'd been so accommodating, so easy, that he'd almost forgotten — Vivienne, before all of that, had been stubborn. She'd had a temper. He sighed and moved toward her. "It's just a bedroom. Come on. We've known Isadora for years. Can't you be a little more flexible?" Vivienne was too tired to keep fighting. She walked out the door. "Vivienne!" He started after her, but a sharp cry from behind stopped him. He turned to find Isadora crumpled on the floor, tears streaming down her face, looking utterly helpless. The baby. He rushed back to her. ****** Vivienne drove to her apartment. The moment she stepped inside and closed the door behind her — her space, only hers — something in her chest finally loosened. She was grateful, now more than ever, that she hadn't listened to Harrison when he'd pushed her to sell this place. If she had, she'd have nowhere to go tonight. He'd bought her other properties over the years, sure. But those were in both their names. Nothing he'd ever given her was fully, cleanly hers. Five years of marriage, and she was only realizing it now. Every gift, every gesture — none of it had ever been unconditional. From the moment he'd tricked her into that fake marriage, he'd been keeping a hand on the door. A cramp twisted through her stomach. She hadn't eaten dinner. The fridge was empty — the apartment had been sitting vacant too long. She picked up her phone and ordered delivery. She needed to take care of herself. candidates.caption: Chapter 1 At 9:02 a.m., my husband fired me from the company I built. At 9:06, he moved his mistress into my office. At 9:09, HR canceled my family's health insurance. At 9:14, security walked me out past two hundred employees. At 9:41, the children's hospital called: my six-year-old daughter's brain surgery — twelve days away — was no longer covered. I didn't scream. I didn't cry. I didn't call him. Because none of them knew the one thing that mattered: I owned sixty-two percent of that company. I stood in the parking garage of Meridian Surgical with a cardboard box in my arms — one photo of Poppy, one dead succulent, a coffee mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST ENGINEER — and I listened to a woman from Brightwater Children's Hospital explain, very gently, that our authorization had been withdrawn. "Mrs. Whitmore, your coverage terminated this morning at 9:09. Without insurance, the hemispherotomy is three hundred forty thousand dollars. We'd need payment or a new plan before we can hold the surgical date." Twelve days. My daughter had waited fourteen months for that date. Poppy has epilepsy. On a good week, four seizures. On a bad week, I don't sleep, because I lie on the floor of her room counting her breaths. The surgery at Brightwater would stop them. Dr. Alvarez said she could be running on a soccer field by spring. "I'll wire it today," I said. "Full amount. Cash." There was a pause. "Ma'am — three hundred forty thousand dollars?" "Today," I said. "By noon." I hung up and wired it from an account my husband had never seen, attached to a name he'd never bothered to look up, and then I sat in my nine-year-old Subaru and stared at my phone until the screen went black. Then I opened Instagram. Because at 9:52, Sienna Voss had already posted. There she was — twenty-seven, glossy, gorgeous — standing in front of a matte-black Range Rover with a red bow on the hood. One hand on the hood. One hand resting, deliberately, on the small curve of her stomach. Caption: "When a man actually shows up for you. ? New car, new office, new everything." New office. I zoomed in on the background. I knew that window. That was the corner window I'd designed the floor plan around, because it caught the morning light and made the prototype lab look like a place where the future got built. That car cost about a hundred and ninety thousand dollars. Company money. My money, if we're being technical, and I am always being technical. Grant Whitmore hadn't fired me because I was underperforming. He'd fired me because the board vote was Friday, and he needed me gone by then. He'd canceled the insurance because a woman with a sick child doesn't have the time or the strength to fight a proxy war. He wanted me buried in hospital paperwork, terrified, begging. He thought that was smart. At 11:40, he texted me. "Babe, I know today was brutal. The board forced my hand — restructuring. Nothing personal, it's just business. We'll get Poppy on my plan, don't spiral. Love you." Nothing personal. I looked at that text for a long time. Then I typed back: "Okay. I understand. It's just business." Three dots. Then: "God, you're incredible. Most women would've made a scene." I put the phone down and I smiled for the first time all morning, and if he'd seen that smile he would have gotten on a plane. Here's what my charming, handsome, Ivy-League husband had somehow forgotten in fourteen months of buying jewelry with the company card: The building Meridian Surgical operates out of? My father's old warehouse. Held in the Quinn Family Trust. My name. I am their landlord. The technology Meridian sells — the Halo navigation array that made him a keynote speaker at three conferences last year? I invented it. The patents are held personally by me and licensed to the company for one dollar a year. Revocable at will. I am their supply chain. And two years ago, when our founding investor got divorced and needed liquidity fast, I quietly bought his entire stake through a holding company called Larkspur. Grant Whitmore doesn't have a wife. He has a landlord, a licensor, and a majority shareholder. And on Friday, all three of them were going to walk into his boardroom. Chapter 2 That night, after Poppy fell asleep with her hand curled around my thumb, I did something I should have done six months ago. I opened her iPad. It's an old one, cracked at the corner, loaded with dinosaur games. It also still syncs to Grant's iCloud, because three years ago he set it up and never bothered to unlink it, and why would he? I was the safe one. The wife who handled pediatric neurology appointments and payroll and never asked questions. The messages loaded. My marriage ended on a screen smeared with a six-year-old's fingerprints. Fourteen months. Hotel charges on Thursdays, when he had "investor dinners." A four-thousand-dollar bracelet in April — the month he told me we needed to be careful about Poppy's out-of-network specialist. A ski weekend in Aspen in January, while I sat in a Brightwater consult room learning the phrase "surgical candidacy." And the texts. Sienna: "does she seriously not suspect anything ?" Grant: "Wren? never. she's too busy playing nurse to the kid." Sienna: "playing nurse is expensive lol. when do I get the title on the car?" Grant: "after Friday. board pushes her out, insurance lapses, and she'll be so buried in hospital bills she won't have the bandwidth to fight anything." She won't have the bandwidth to fight anything. I sat on the edge of my daughter's bed, in the house I paid for, and read a man calmly plan to use my child's illness as a strategy. Let me tell you what the last eight years actually looked like. When I met Grant, he was a mediocre medical device salesman with charm for days and ninety-one thousand dollars in debt. I paid it off. When I built the Halo prototype in my father's warehouse — a warehouse that still smelled like sawdust and my dead dad's aftershave — Grant said, "You're the brain, I'm the mouth." I liked that. I believed it. I put my entire inheritance into Meridian. Four hundred thousand dollars. I wrote the code. I filed the patents. I hired the first eleven employees and made payroll out of my own account for nineteen months. And Grant went to conferences and said "we" a lot, and everyone decided he was the founder, and I let them, because I thought it didn't matter who got the applause as long as we got the life. His mother, Adele Whitmore, sat me down at our rehearsal dinner, patted my hand, and said, "You understand you're marrying up, dear. The Whitmores have been in this city four generations." I paid for that wedding. Every plate. And my mother — Dot, five-foot-two, in her one good dress — sat at a corner table while Adele introduced her to exactly nobody. Later I heard Adele by the coat check, laughing with a friend. "The mother cleaned motel rooms. Motel rooms, can you imagine. Bad blood in that family, if you ask me. Thank God the girl is useful." Bad blood. My mother raised me alone after my father died on a job site. She cleaned rooms at the Sundowner Inn for twenty-two years so I could take AP physics instead of a shift. She has never once asked me for anything. I kept scrolling. My hands were completely steady. Screenshots. Cloud backup. Two copies. Three. Timestamps intact, metadata preserved, the way Priya taught me years ago when she drafted my patent license and said, "Someday you'll be glad this is airtight." And then I reached the last exchange, sent forty minutes before I opened the iPad. Sienna: "I sat in her chair today. It's comfy ?" Grant: "told you. one more week." Sienna: "the baby won't wait forever. And neither will Vantage." I read that line six times. The baby, I'd already accepted. Ugly, but simple. But Vantage? Vantage Medical was our competitor. Our biggest one. The company that had tried to buy my patents twice and been told no twice — by me. Why was my husband's pregnant mistress talking about Vantage like it was a deadline? I put the iPad back on the charger, exactly where I'd found it, the way a good wife does. Then I went to the kitchen table, opened my laptop, and pulled up three documents: a trust deed, a patent license agreement, and a cap table with sixty-two percent of Meridian Surgical sitting under a holding company called Larkspur. By sunrise, I wasn't a wife anymore. I was a countdown. Chapter 3 They came to the hospital two days later. Not to see Poppy. Let's be clear about that. We were at Brightwater for her pre-op workup — twelve hours of EEG leads glued to my daughter's scalp, a bright pink hospital gown, a cartoon dinosaur on the ceiling tile above her bed. She was watching a tablet with the sound off, tapping her foot, brave in a way that breaks you. Adele Whitmore swept into the pediatric neurology ward in a cream Chanel jacket, her son trailing behind her with a leather folder, and neither of them so much as glanced at Room 412. "Wren." Adele air-kissed the space beside my face. "Somewhere private, please. This floor smells like sick children." We sat in the family consultation room. Grant wouldn't look at me. Adele had no such problem. "I'll be direct, because I respect you," she said, in the tone of a woman who has never respected anyone in her life. "Sienna Voss is pregnant. It's a boy. He'll be a Whitmore." She said it like a title of nobility. "Grant needs a divorce. Quick and quiet, before the board vote." She slid the folder across the table. "We've had papers drawn. Very generous, considering." I opened it. I would walk away with my clothes, my nine-year-old Subaru, and a "goodwill payment" of fifteen thousand dollars. The house, the accounts, and all "company interests" would remain with Grant. The house I bought. The accounts I filled. The company that exists because I built a machine in my dead father's warehouse. "Sign it," Adele said, "and we keep this civilized. Fight it, and I promise you, the Whitmore name carries weight in this city. You'll leave with nothing, and everyone will know exactly why." I looked at Grant. "Anything to add?" He finally met my eyes, and he had the audacity to look wounded. Gentle. Like a man putting down an old dog. "Wren, you've been a good partner. Genuinely. But Sienna and I — it's real. And she's giving me a son." A pause. "You were always so consumed. With the lab. With Poppy's appointments. Maybe if things had been different..." Maybe if things had been different. I paid off his debt. I invented his product. I made payroll from my personal savings for nineteen months while he learned to golf. I funded the Range Rover he gave his pregnant mistress on the same morning he canceled his own daughter's insurance. And our marriage died because I took our sick child to too many doctors. Adele leaned in, lowering her voice like she was doing me a favor. "And dear — about the girl. All this medical drama. That's a Quinn problem now, not a Whitmore problem. Frankly, faulty wiring runs in certain families. Sienna's people are healthy stock. You understand." Faulty wiring. My daughter was thirty feet away with electrodes glued to her head, and this woman was discussing her like a defective appliance. Something inside me went very, very still. The same stillness I'd felt in that parking garage. I closed the folder. "I'll sign," I said. Grant's head snapped up. Adele blinked, then bloomed into a triumphant smile. "Well. Finally. Sense." "I need until Friday," I said. "To review it properly. You understand — I'd hate to miss any details." "Friday's the board meeting," Grant said quickly. "Then it's a big week for both of us." "Of course, of course." Adele was already standing, smoothing her jacket, victory perfuming the air. "See, Grant? I told you she'd be practical. She always was the practical type." They left without asking my daughter's name. In three years of marriage, Adele Whitmore had never once said the word "Poppy" out loud. I stood alone in that consultation room and watched them walk to the elevators — Adele laughing at something, Grant already texting, probably Sienna, probably "it's done, baby." Then I took out my phone and called a number I'd kept for exactly this day. "Priya Raman." "It's Wren. Remember the file I sent you two years ago? The one you called my 'break glass in case of husband'?" A pause. Then, softly: "He finally did it, didn't he." "He finally did it." "Say the word and I file everything Monday morning." I watched the elevator doors close on my husband's smiling face. "File it all," I said. "The license. The lease. The Larkspur stake. Every page." By Friday, Grant Whitmore would own nothing but his last name. He just didn't know it yet.
